extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of advertising history; general readers interested in historical examples of advertisements
extracted.subtask_description: Selection and commentary on curious and eccentric 19th-century advertisements, illustrating recurring requirements, tactics, and social implications of advertising copy of the period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product authenticity and awards
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of medals/awards and claims of superior preference to assert product quality and authenticity (e.g., 'MEDAILLE of SILVER at New-York. MEDAILLE of GOLD at Paris, London and Berlin. The very celebrated AMERICAN-BALSAM... preserve the preference').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advertisers invoke international medals and customer preference to signal legitimacy; include statements preventing imitation (e.g., sole agent notices) and contractual promises (example: 'NO HAIR NO MONNEY') to reassure buyers and deter counterfeiters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sole agent / anti-imitation notice
rubrics_metrics.description: Declare a sole agent for a territory and warn against imitation (example: 'THEOPHILE is sole agent for the Netherlands, St. Nicholasstreet at Amsterdam').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use explicit territorial agency claims and bold directives to prevent imitation and direct purchasers to the authorized seller.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chaperon candidate qualifications
rubrics_metrics.description: Detailed personal and behavioral requirements for a chaperon: 'must possess a constitution impervious to fatigue and heat, and be perfectly independent of sleep; fit at the mysteries of Whist and Cassino, and always ready to undertake a round game... any personal charms... will be deemed inadmissible; must be totally divested of matrimonial pretensions... sufficient experience in the beati monde to decide with promptitude on the eligibility of invitations...'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ads for social servants specify precise temperament, leisure/party-related skills, and social discretion; explicitly exclude attributes that might compete with charges (anti-pattern: advertising personal charms).

rubrics_metrics.name: School assistant subject requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Employment ad specifying instructional scope: 'Wanted, a respectable GENTLEMAN of good character, capable of TEACHING THE CLASSICS as far as Homer and Virgil.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Set explicit curricular endpoints (named authors) to define expected competency; the text records how such requirements could be mocked/misread (hoax letter joking about distance to 'Homer and Virgil').

rubrics_metrics.name: Minister for fashionable chapel — social requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Hire specification for a fashionable chapel minister: 'a gentleman of elegant manners, and insinuating address... not necessary that he believe in the Thirty-nine Articles; expected to possess a white hand and a diamond ring; leave out vulgar ideas... on no account be guilty of wounding the ears of his auditory with the words h—ll or d—n; one who lisps, is near-sighted, and who has a due regard for amiable weaknesses, will be preferred.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ads may prioritize social polish, appearance, and the suppression of 'vulgar' religious content over doctrinal fidelity or preaching duties; explicitly list mannerisms and physical quirks as desirable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Servant: polyvalent confidential qualities
rubrics_metrics.description: Self-advertised servant offering wide-ranging, non-menial services: 'offers his services... truly faithful, confidential servant in any capacity not menial... practical knowledge of human nature... has never been a servant... is moral, temperate, middle-aged... can give advice or hold his tongue, sing, dance, play, fence, box, preach a sermon... never to excel his master.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such ads promote extreme versatility, social polish, and discretion; the copy highlights claims to mixed elite/social experience as a selling point.

rubrics_metrics.name: Companion/factotum candidate profile
rubrics_metrics.description: Candidate who wants to be companion/factotum: 'can produce a cubic yard of testimonials, a living without a master... can ride, shoot, sing, fish... keep accounts, see that servants do their duty... and make it his whole duty to please and be pleased.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advertisers enumerate practical leisure and household management skills while promising subordination and social compatibility; testimonials and claims of independence are emphasized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employer conditions for board-for-work offers
rubrics_metrics.description: Employer posting conditional offers of board/residence in exchange for labor: 'invites two widow ladies, about forty, to assist him in doing without servants... one lady must undertake entrees, soups, and jellies... both must be strong and healthy... laundry free... references of mercantile exactness required.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ads frame unpaid or low-paid domestic labor as exchange for room and board; require health, references, and list duties—author warns such offers often mask attempts to obtain servants without wages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Governess qualifications and exploitative terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Governess ad specifying teaching and domestic responsibilities: 'a young lady, as NURSERY GOVERNESS, to instruct two young ladies in French, music, and singing, with the usual branches... to take the entire charge of their wardrobe... social disposition and fond of children, and have the manners of a gentlewoman... Salary twelve guineas per annum.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text criticizes how ads disguise drudgery as 'one of the family' and how minimal salary is expected despite extensive duties; 'manners of a gentlewoman' is read as expectation of patient endurance of insult and extra unpaid tasks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demoiselle de compagnie specifications
rubrics_metrics.description: Ad seeking a young girl of good family for companionship: 'must be well educated, accomplished, and of an agreeable figure... will be entertained in the quality of demoiselle de compagnie... receive the utmost attention... as well served... as, or even better than, if she were its mistress.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ads for companion roles emphasize family background, education, accomplishment, and appearance, promising preferential domestic treatment as incentive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural/legal claims in public notices (pavement/accident claims)
rubrics_metrics.description: Solicitors' public notice requesting 'PROVED ACCOUNTS in writing of all ACCIDENTS to and DEATHS of HORSES, and Personal and other Casualties... within one calendar month of our respective applications' to pursue extra-judicial or court actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legal/claims-oriented adverts function as calls for documented evidence within strict timeframes and set out consequences (court proceedings), serving as procedural requirements for prospective claimants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal name-change notice requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Public legal notice of assumed new name with deed poll and enrollment: example includes date of change, request to be addressed by new name, and statement that necessary Deed Poll has been executed and enrolled in the High Court of Chancery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such notices specify legal formalities (deed poll, court enrollment) and a public request that third parties adopt the new name—used to effect and publicize legal identity changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appearance prioritized over formal qualifications
rubrics_metrics.description: Hiring preference that prioritizes appearance: 'appearance is the chief object... where he stated that he was a Cambridge man... as appearance is the chief object.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The historical commentary notes employers sometimes value appearance (dress, bearing) above actual skill or education; an anti‑pattern when competence is needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of memorials/tombstones as advertising medium
rubrics_metrics.description: Creative tactic of erecting a conspicuous monument with an inscription that serves as advertisement (example: fictitious 'Pierre Cabochard' tomb concluding with 'and continues the same business at the old stand, 187, Rue Mouffetard').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unconventional physical displays (even pseudo-memorials) can attract curiosity and direct customers to a business; the author gives a successful grocer example where a fake tomb yielded business.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of personal/death notices to announce business continuity or relocation
rubrics_metrics.description: Death notice that simultaneously informs of business continuity and relocation: 'This bereavement will not interrupt our employment which will be carried on as usual, only our place of business will be removed from No. 3... to No. 4... as our grasping landlord has raised our rent.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combining personal notices with practical business information is a tactic to capitalize on readership sympathy/attention while communicating operational details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeals to sympathy and social rank to solicit funds
rubrics_metrics.description: Personal appeals for financial assistance framed by claims of rank/education and assurances of secrecy but offering no security: 'A MAN OF RANK... has been suddenly called upon to pay some thousands of pounds... he can offer no adequate security... address to "Anxious"...' and similar appeals promising gratitude and secrecy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such ads exploit perceived status and pathos to solicit funds; the text notes declining effectiveness over time unless something is promised in return; these appeals can be genuine or manipulative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improbable promises as a swindler's technique
rubrics_metrics.description: Observation that swindling advertisements often succeed by offering highly improbable undertakings; 'if we are to judge by most of the swindling advertisements which have succeeded... the more improbable the undertaking the more probable the success.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make-of-it lesson: extravagant, unlikely claims can draw victims; this is recorded as a historical pattern of fraudulent advertising tactics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offering social entrée in exchange for hospitality/services
rubrics_metrics.description: Ads offering free lodging and expenses to individuals of family or rank in return for providing entrée into high society ('offer to RECEIVE as their GUEST, free of all expense, a lady or gentleman of family, who, in sole return for the freedom of home, could give the entree into Belgian society').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advertisers promise coveted social access as the advertised commodity; the author remarks these notices suggest bribery or social climbing and were placed in fashionable papers to reach desired audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selling 'secret' national remedies for a fee
rubrics_metrics.description: Grandiose political/policy proposals offered to government or wealthy patrons in exchange for large upfront payment: 'A Remedy for the distresses of England... The advertiser will communicate his discovery... on condition of his receiving... £100,000.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ads of grand schemes solicit large payments for 'discoveries' or plans claimed to be practicable; they typically promise sweeping social benefits while demanding exclusive payment for disclosure—a classic speculative/tactical advertisement form.
